blocks.text: THE OLD ASSUMPTION: TO VERIFY THE FACT, YOU MUST SEE THE DATA. ZERO KNOWLEDGE BREAKS THAT ASSUMPTION.
VERIFICATION USED TO COME WITH A DISCLOSURE BILL.

Financial systems constantly ask for evidence. Do you own the funds? Is the transaction balanced? Are you authorized to spend? Traditional verification often answers those questions by exposing the underlying information to whoever performs the check.

Zero-knowledge proof systems create a different possibility: convince a verifier that a statement is valid without revealing the secret information — the witness — used to establish it, beyond what follows from the statement being true.
01 // STATEMENT VS. WITNESS

The Halo 2 documentation describes an argument of knowledge using a public statement x and a witness w related by some efficiently checkable relation. The prover knows the witness. The verifier needs confidence that an appropriate witness exists and is known, but does not necessarily need to receive that witness.
That separation is the conceptual move. The verifier can check the proof instead of demanding the private inputs themselves.
THE SECRET IS USED TO CREATE THE PROOF. THE SECRET DOES NOT HAVE TO BECOME THE PROOF.
02 // FOUR QUESTIONS A PROOF SYSTEM HAS TO ANSWER

The Halo 2 protocol description separates several security notions. Completeness asks whether an honest prover with a valid witness can convince the verifier. Soundness asks whether a cheating prover can convince the verifier of a false statement. Knowledge soundness asks whether acceptance implies the prover actually possesses an appropriate witness. Zero knowledge asks what the verifier learns beyond the validity of the statement and the prover's knowledge of a witness.
Those properties are related but not interchangeable. A proof can be convincing without being zero knowledge. Zero knowledge is the additional property that changes the disclosure model.
03 // WHAT THIS MEANS INSIDE ORCHARD

Zcash Orchard uses Halo 2 as part of its shielded protocol. Orchard represents shielded transfers using Actions. Each Action combines a spend side and an output side, and the protocol uses commitments, nullifiers, signatures and zero-knowledge proofs so that consensus can enforce the required rules without publishing the underlying note data as ordinary transparent transaction fields.

A nullifier allows the network to detect an attempt to spend the same shielded note again without publicly identifying the note in the way a transparent UTXO reference would. Commitments bind hidden data. The proof demonstrates that the relevant constraints were satisfied. These pieces work together; the zero-knowledge proof is not a magical encryption layer acting alone.
04 // HIDDEN DOES NOT MEAN UNVERIFIED

This is the part that often gets lost in arguments about private cryptocurrency. Public visibility and public verifiability are not the same property. A system can conceal selected transaction details while still giving validators cryptographic evidence that the transaction obeys its consensus rules.
The rules are not secret. The verification algorithm is not secret. What changes is whether every private input required to satisfy those rules must also become public data.
TRANSPARENCY OF RULES DOES NOT REQUIRE TRANSPARENCY OF EVERY PRIVATE INPUT.
05 // ZERO KNOWLEDGE DOES NOT HIDE EVERYTHING

The phrase zero knowledge is easy to overread. It does not mean that an observer learns literally nothing about a transaction. The public statement, transaction structure and protocol-defined public inputs still exist. Fees can remain visible. Moving value across shielded-pool boundaries can reveal information. Network metadata exists outside the proof system entirely.

ZIP 224 gives a concrete Orchard example: spending funds from Orchard to a non-Orchard address reveals the value transferred across that boundary. That is not a failure of Halo 2. It is a consequence of what the surrounding transaction protocol deliberately makes public.
06 // THE QUESTION CHANGED

Before zero-knowledge systems, the instinctive architecture was often disclosure first: reveal the inputs, then let everyone recompute the answer. Zero knowledge adds another design space. Define exactly what must be proven. Keep the witness private. Publish enough cryptographic evidence for the verifier to accept or reject the claim.
That is bigger than a privacy feature. It changes what verification can mean.
DON'T SHOW ME THE SECRET. SHOW ME THAT THE RULES WERE SATISFIED.
SOURCES // VERIFY IT YOURSELF
ZEROTRACE //
Verification used to ask for the evidence. Zero knowledge asks a harder question: how little evidence can you reveal and still prove the truth?
